keyQuotes: Exercise buys you roughly 3.5 extra years of life - probably the largest reliable gain in longevity available to you right now.
If you dislike sports, you should probably still put in a couple of hours a week.
Once you have enough exercise, you have enough.

mainPoints.explanation: The effect is huge – more than many interventions – but plateaus: beyond 5-12 hours per week (depending on intensity), additional exercise neither helps nor harms mortality risk.
mainPoints.point: Regular exercise extends life by roughly 3.5 years, likely the largest reliable longevity gain available.

mainPoints.explanation: High-intensity exercise delivers more benefit per minute, so if you're going to suffer, suffer briefly and get large benefits. Low-intensity is worth it only if you enjoy it, otherwise it requires too many painful hours.
mainPoints.point: People who dislike exercise should still do a moderate amount, but intensity matters.

mainPoints.explanation: If you find other activities more enjoyable than exercise, the optimal trade-off may be slightly less exercise than the health-optimal level, balancing extra hours of life against lower quality of those hours.
mainPoints.point: The model explicitly accounts for utility (enjoyment) of exercise, not just health benefits.

mainPoints.explanation: Going from hating to loving exercise provides a huge gain, equivalent to many years of life. Public health insurers should theoretically pay tens of thousands of dollars to make that happen.
mainPoints.point: Investing in finding a sport you love can be worth ~2.5 quality-adjusted life years.

mainPoints.explanation: The author multiplies the published effect by 0.7 to adjust for observational bias, and notes that baseline mortality changes do not meaningfully alter the relative recommendations.
mainPoints.point: The calculator is a rough tool, not a precise medical prediction, but robust to assumption changes.

oneSentenceSummary: This article analyzes the longevity benefits of exercise, presents a calculator to determine optimal exercise levels based on individual preferences and health data, and offers practical takeaways for both exercise lovers and haters.
summary: Based on a recent meta-analysis on leisure exercise and longevity, the author builds an interactive calculator to estimate how much exercise is optimal for an individual, factoring in not only the health benefits (~3.5 extra years of life) but also how much one enjoys or dislikes exercise. Key findings: benefits plateau at roughly 5-12 hours per week; those who hate exercise should still do a few hours weekly, with higher intensity offering more benefit per minute; finding a sport you love yields a huge improvement in quality-adjusted life years (~2.5 life-year equivalents). The article includes caveats about observational bias and age effects, providing a nuanced, rational framework for exercise decisions.
title: Optimal Exercise Calculator
